name: Klein Steel Climbers with T-Pads
title: Klein Steel Climbers with T-Pads: Fit, Gaffs & Care
meta: Klein steel climbers with T-pads: adjustable steel shanks, replaceable gaffs and padded uppers for removals and pole work. Fit, gaff care and buying notes.
tagline: Durable adjustable steel climbers with T-style pads for removal and utility climbers.
summary: Klein steel climbers with T-pads pair adjustable steel shanks and replaceable gaffs with padded upper cuffs that spread the load across the calf. They suit climbers who want a rugged, no-nonsense spur for removals and line-clearance style work.
highlights: Adjustable steel shanks to match leg length
T-style pads spread pressure across the calf
Steel build that takes jobsite abuse
For removals only, never for pruning live trees

body.h: Where steel climbers earn their keep
p: Steel climbers are heavier than aluminum or carbon spurs, but they shrug off being thrown in a truck box, kicked through bark all day and stood on hard while you make a face cut aloft. For a removal climber or utility crew that prizes durability over shaving ounces, a steel set with good pads is still a sound pick.

The T-pads wrap the upper calf and spread the load from the shank so long days on spikes are less punishing. Get the shank length right first: the top of the shank should sit an inch or two below the knee so it doesn't dig in when you bend. Browse other options in our climbing spurs range.

Gaff condition is the whole game on spurs. A dull or badly shaped gaff can cut out, so keep a gauge handy, sharpen with a file only (no grinders, which can draw the temper), and replace gaffs once they are worn short. Check straps, buckles and pads for cuts and wear before each climb.

Spurs are for removals, not pruning, because every gaff wound is an entry point for decay. Follow the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, always climb with a lanyard or flipline set, and get trained before relying on spikes. Replacement gaffs and parts are in replacement gaffs and parts.

faq.q: Are Klein steel climbers good for tree work?
faq.a: They are a durable option for removals. Make sure the gaff style suits trees, keep gaffs sharp and always climb with a lanyard.

faq.q: Can I replace the gaffs on these climbers?
faq.a: Yes, the gaffs are replaceable. Use gaffs made for this climber and follow Klein's fitting instructions.

name: Distel Carbon 3 V 2020 Tree Gaffs with Velcro Straps
title: Distel Carbon 3 V 2020 Spurs with Velcro Straps
meta: Distel Carbon spurs (3 V 2020) with Velcro straps: very light carbon-shank climbers for removal climbers who spike all day. Fit, gaff care and buying notes.
tagline: Light carbon-shank tree spurs from Distel for climbers who spend all day on gaffs.
summary: The Distel carbon spurs in the 3 V 2020 version use carbon fiber shanks to cut weight on your legs, with Velcro straps for quick, even adjustment. They are aimed at production removal climbers who feel every ounce by the end of a long take-down.
highlights: Carbon fiber shanks keep weight down
Velcro straps for quick, even tension
A premium pick for full-time removal climbers

p: Lighter spurs mean less fatigue climbing a long spar and less swing when you step around the stem. Carbon shanks are stiff and light, and Distel's design keeps the gaff in line with your leg so it bites cleanly instead of rolling out.

The Velcro straps make it fast to snug the lower and upper straps evenly, which helps the spur sit still on your boot. Pair them with a good boot that has a solid shank and instep. See the rest of our lightweight spurs for aluminum and other options.

Carbon is tough in normal use but does not like sharp impacts against steel or rock. Inspect the shanks for cracks, chips or delamination before each climb and retire any part that looks damaged. Keep the gaffs sharp with a file and a gauge, and replace them when worn short.
Spurs are for removals only, never for pruning live trees. Follow Distel's instructions and ANSI Z133, always use a lanyard or flipline while spiking, and be trained before climbing on gaffs.

faq.q: Are Distel carbon spurs worth the price?
faq.a: For climbers who spike most days, the weight savings add up. Occasional users may get better value from aluminum spurs.

faq.q: Can I fit replacement gaffs to Distel carbon spurs?
faq.a: Yes. Use genuine Distel-compatible gaffs and check the fit for your model before climbing.

name: Adjustable Climber Sleeve for Buckingham Steel Climbers
title: Buckingham Adjustable Climber Sleeve for Steel Spurs
h1: Adjustable Climber Sleeve for Buckingham Steel Climbers
meta: Replacement Buckingham climber sleeve for adjustable steel climbers. Restore height adjustment on worn spurs and get the shank sitting right below the knee.
tagline: Replacement adjustable sleeve that restores height adjustment on Buckingham steel spurs.
summary: This Buckingham climber sleeve replaces the adjustable upper section on Buckingham steel climbers, so you can set the shank height to your leg again. It is a parts-level fix that keeps a good set of spurs in service.
highlights: Made for Buckingham adjustable steel climbers
Cheaper than a new set of spurs

p: The adjustable sleeve takes a beating, and worn or bent holes, stripped hardware or a sleeve that won't lock at the right height mean it is time for a new one. A shank that sits too high digs into the back of the knee; too low and the spur feels sloppy. Getting the height right is as much about safety as comfort.
Confirm your climber model before ordering, since sleeves are not universal between brands or even between product lines. Browse other parts in replacement gaffs and parts.

Fit the sleeve with the correct Buckingham screws, tighten to snug, and check that the shank cannot slip under load. Set the height so the top of the shank sits a little below the knee with your boot on.

After any repair, inspect the whole spur, including gaffs, straps and pads, before climbing. Follow the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, and if anything about the repair is in doubt, have a qualified person check it or retire the spur.

faq.q: Will this sleeve fit other brands of climbers?
faq.a: No. It is made for Buckingham adjustable steel climbers. Check your model first.

faq.q: Do I need new screws with the sleeve?
faq.a: Replace screws that are worn or stripped. Use the correct Buckingham hardware for your model.

name: Buckingham Gaff Shaping Gauge
title: Buckingham Gaff Shaping Gauge for Sharpening Spurs
meta: Buckingham gaff gauge for checking and shaping climber gaffs while you file. Keeps tree gaff profile and length right so spurs bite and don't cut out.
tagline: A simple template that keeps your spur gaffs filed to the right shape.
summary: The Buckingham gaff gauge is a profile template you hold against your climber gaffs while sharpening, so you file them back to the correct shape and know when they are worn too short. It takes the guesswork out of spur maintenance.
highlights: Shows when gaffs are too short to keep using
Pocket-size, lives in the spur bag

p: A gaff that is filed too thin, too blunt or at the wrong angle can roll out of the bark and drop you onto your lanyard. Most cut-outs trace back to gaffs that were sharpened by eye on a grinder until the profile was gone. A gauge gives you a fixed reference every time.

Sharpen with a fine flat file on the outside faces only, checking against the gauge as you go. Never use a bench grinder, which can overheat the steel and ruin the temper. More spur parts are in replacement gaffs and parts.

body.h: Know when to retire a gaff
p: Every sharpening takes a little length. When the gauge shows the gaff is short of the minimum, replace it rather than squeezing out another week. Short gaffs don't penetrate far enough to hold on thick-barked trees.
Check gaffs before each climb and after hitting anything hard, like wire, nails or rock. Follow the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133 for spur use and maintenance.

faq.q: Can I use this gauge on non-Buckingham gaffs?
faq.a: It is designed for Buckingham gaffs. Other brands may use a different profile, so check with that maker's guidance.

faq.q: Should I sharpen gaffs with a grinder?
faq.a: No. Use a file. Grinders can overheat the steel and change the profile.

name: Climb Right Replacement Gaffs
title: Climb Right Replacement Gaffs for Tree Climbers
meta: Climb Right replacement gaffs for Climb Right tree climbers. Swap worn or damaged gaffs and keep your spurs biting clean on removals. Fit and care tips.
tagline: Fresh tree gaffs to bring a worn set of Climb Right spurs back into service.
summary: Climb Right replacement gaffs let you swap out worn or damaged gaffs on Climb Right climbers instead of buying a new set of spurs. Fresh gaffs bite cleaner and are far less likely to cut out.
highlights: Keeps a good set of spurs working

p: Gaffs wear with every sharpening. Once they are short, chipped, bent or the profile can't be filed back, the spur won't penetrate thick bark reliably. That is when cut-outs happen. Replacing gaffs is cheap compared with the alternative.
Confirm your Climb Right model before ordering, since gaffs are model-specific. You'll find more spur parts in replacement gaffs and parts.
Fit the gaffs with the correct hardware and tighten fully, then check there is no play. Keep them sharp with a file, checking the profile against a gauge, and never use a grinder.
Spurs are for removals only. Inspect gaffs, straps and pads before each climb, use a lanyard or flipline while spiking, and follow the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133.

faq.q: Will Climb Right gaffs fit other brands?
faq.a: They are made for Climb Right climbers. Don't mix gaffs and climbers from different makers unless the manufacturer says they fit.

faq.q: Should I replace both gaffs at once?
faq.a: Yes, replacing them as a pair keeps both feet biting the same way.

name: Climb Right Steel Height Adjustment Sleeve and Screws
title: Climb Right Steel Height Adjustment Sleeve & Screws
h1: Climb Right Steel Height Adjustment Sleeve and Screws
meta: Climb Right steel adjustment sleeve with screws for adjustable climbers. Replace a worn sleeve and get spur shank height dialed in for your leg again.
tagline: Replacement height sleeve and hardware for adjustable Climb Right steel climbers.
summary: This Climb Right adjustment sleeve comes with its screws and replaces the height-adjusting section on Climb Right steel climbers. Swap it when holes wear, hardware strips or the shank won't hold its setting.
highlights: Sleeve and screws in one kit
For adjustable Climb Right steel climbers

p: The sleeve sets how high the shank rides on your leg. Too high and it digs in behind the knee every time you bend; too low and the spur feels loose and less stable. When holes elongate or screws strip, you lose that adjustment and the spur can shift.
Check your climber model before ordering. More Climb Right and other parts are in replacement gaffs and parts.

Remove the old sleeve, fit the new one with the supplied screws and tighten firmly. Set height with your work boot on so the top of the shank sits a little below the knee, then confirm nothing moves under load.
After any repair, inspect the whole spur before climbing. Follow the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, and have a qualified person check the work if you are unsure.

faq.q: Are screws included?
faq.a: Yes, this kit includes the sleeve and the screws.

faq.q: Will it fit Climb Right aluminum climbers?
faq.a: It is listed for Climb Right steel climbers. Check your model before ordering.

name: Climb Right Ultralight Pad Screws
title: Climb Right Ultralight Pad Screws for Climber Pads
meta: Replacement Climb Right Ultralight pad screws to reattach climber pads to the shank. Replace lost or stripped screws before they let a pad shift mid-climb.
tagline: Spare screws to keep the pads tight on Climb Right Ultralight climbers.
summary: Climb Right Ultralight pad screws are the small replacement fasteners that hold the pads to the shanks on Climb Right Ultralight climbers. Lost or stripped pad screws are a common nuisance, and a spare set keeps your spurs ready.
highlights: Made for Climb Right Ultralight climbers
Replace lost or stripped pad screws
Small part worth keeping in the gear bag

p: A pad that shifts on the shank puts pressure in the wrong place and can make the spur feel unstable. Pad screws vibrate loose, strip or simply go missing when you swap pads. Keeping a few spares in the climbing bag saves a job from being cut short.
These are sized for Climb Right Ultralight climbers. Check your model, and see replacement gaffs and parts for other spur hardware.

body.h: Check them as part of inspection
p: Make pad screws part of your pre-climb spur check along with gaffs, straps and buckles. Snug them firmly but don't overtighten into the pad.
If a screw hole is stripped or the pad mount is damaged, don't improvise. Follow the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, and retire or repair the spur properly before climbing on it.

faq.q: Will these screws fit other climbers?
faq.a: They are made for Climb Right Ultralight climbers. Other brands may use a different thread or length.

faq.q: Should I use thread locker on pad screws?
faq.a: Follow Climb Right's instructions. If they don't call for it, just check the screws regularly.

name: Distel Eye Bolt M8x11
title: Distel Eye Bolt M8x11 Replacement Spur Part
meta: Distel eye bolt M8x11, a genuine replacement part for Distel climbers. Swap a worn or lost bolt and keep your spurs complete. Fit and inspection notes.
tagline: Genuine Distel M8 eye bolt for keeping your Distel spurs complete and serviceable.
summary: The Distel eye bolt M8x11 is a small replacement part for Distel climbers, used where the spur's strap or fitting attaches. Replace one that is worn, bent or lost instead of improvising with hardware-store bolts.
highlights: Replace worn, bent or missing bolts

p: Spur hardware sees a lot of vibration and load. A generic eye bolt may look the same but differ in thread length, material or strength. Using the genuine Distel part keeps the spur working as designed.
Check your Distel model and the part location against Distel's documentation before ordering. Other spur parts are in replacement gaffs and parts.
Thread the bolt in fully and check that it is tight and sitting square. Look over the surrounding strap and fittings while you are at it.
Inspect all spur hardware before each climb. If you are unsure whether a repair is sound, have a qualified person check it. Follow Distel's instructions and ANSI Z133.

faq.q: Can I use a hardware-store M8 eye bolt instead?
faq.a: Use the genuine Distel part. Generic bolts may differ in length, material or strength.

faq.q: Which Distel climbers use this bolt?
faq.a: Check Distel's parts information for your model before ordering.

name: Klein Replacement Gaffs
title: Klein Replacement Gaffs for Klein Climbers
meta: Klein replacement gaffs for Klein climbers. Swap worn-short or chipped gaffs so your spurs bite cleanly again. Check your model and gaff style first.
tagline: Replacement gaffs to restore grip on worn Klein climbers.
summary: Klein replacement gaffs fit Klein climbers and let you replace gaffs that are worn short, chipped or bent instead of buying new spurs. Match the gaff style to your climber and the work you do.
highlights: Fit with the correct Klein hardware

p: Klein builds climbers for both pole and tree use, and the gaffs differ. Tree gaffs are longer to get through thick bark into wood; pole gaffs are shorter. Check which climber you have and which gaff it needs before ordering.
More spur parts are in replacement gaffs and parts, and full sets are under climbing spurs.
Fit gaffs with the correct hardware, tighten fully and check for play. Keep them sharp with a file and a gauge, never a grinder, and retire them once they wear short.
Inspect gaffs and straps before every climb. Use spurs only for removals or utility work, always climb with a lanyard, and follow Klein's instructions and ANSI Z133.

faq.q: Can I put tree gaffs on Klein pole climbers?
faq.a: Only if Klein lists them as compatible with your model. Check before ordering.

faq.q: How do I know when to replace gaffs?
faq.a: Replace them when they are worn short, chipped or bent, or when a gauge shows the profile can't be restored.

name: Replacement Gaffs for Distel and Gecko Climbers
title: Distel Replacement Gaffs for Distel & Gecko Spurs
h1: Replacement Gaffs for Distel and Gecko Climbers
meta: Distel replacement gaffs that fit Distel and Gecko climbers. Swap worn-short or damaged gaffs and keep your spurs biting clean on long removal days.
tagline: Tree gaffs that bring worn Distel and Gecko spurs back to full bite.
summary: These Distel replacement gaffs fit both Distel and Gecko climbers, so you can swap worn or damaged gaffs and keep your spurs in service. Fresh gaffs are the single biggest factor in how securely a spur holds.
highlights: Keeps premium spurs working for years

p: Gaffs lose length with each sharpening and take damage from hidden nails, wire and grit. Once they are short or the profile is gone, they can roll out of the bark. On a spur as expensive as a Distel or Gecko, replacing the gaffs is the obvious way to keep it going.
Confirm your model before ordering. Other spur parts are in replacement gaffs and parts.
Fit the gaffs with the correct hardware and tighten fully, then check for any play. Sharpen with a file only and check the profile against a gauge.
Inspect gaffs before each climb and after any hard strike. Spurs are for removals only. Use a lanyard or flipline, and follow the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133.

faq.q: Do these gaffs fit both Distel and Gecko spurs?
faq.a: Yes, they are listed for both. Check your specific model before ordering.

faq.q: Do they come as a pair?
faq.a: Check the listing. Replacing both gaffs together keeps the bite even on both feet.

name: Replacement Gaffs for Tree Hog Aluminum Climbers
title: Replacement Gaffs for Tree Hog Aluminum Climbers
h1: Replacement Gaffs for Tree Hog Aluminum Climbers
meta: Replacement gaffs for Tree Hog aluminum climbers. Swap worn or chipped gaffs so your lightweight spurs bite cleanly again. Fit, sharpening and care tips.
tagline: Replacement tree gaffs for keeping Tree Hog aluminum spurs in service.
summary: These Tree Hog replacement gaffs fit Tree Hog aluminum climbers, letting you replace worn, chipped or bent gaffs without replacing the whole spur. A fresh pair restores the bite you need on thick-barked removals.
highlights: Made for Tree Hog aluminum climbers
Cheaper than a new set of spurs

p: Aluminum shanks save weight, but the gaffs are still steel and still wear. When they are short, chipped or bent, swap them. Confirm the gaff matches your Tree Hog model before ordering.
Other spur parts are in replacement gaffs and parts.
Fit the gaffs with the correct hardware and tighten fully. Sharpen with a file only, checking the profile as you go, and retire gaffs that are worn short.
Inspect gaffs, straps and pads before each climb. Use spurs only on removals, always with a lanyard or flipline, and follow the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133.

faq.q: Will these gaffs fit other aluminum climbers?
faq.a: They are made for Tree Hog aluminum climbers. Don't fit them to other brands unless the maker confirms compatibility.

faq.q: Can I sharpen these with a grinder?
faq.a: No. Use a file to avoid overheating the steel and changing the profile.

name: Weaver Padded Shank Cover
title: Weaver Padded Shank Cover for Climbing Spurs
meta: Weaver padded shank cover cushions the inside of your leg against the climber shank. A simple comfort upgrade for long removal days on spurs. Fit tips.
tagline: Padding that sits between the spur shank and your leg for all-day comfort.
summary: The Weaver shank cover adds padding along the climber shank so the steel or aluminum isn't rubbing the inside of your leg all day. It is a simple comfort upgrade for removal climbers.
highlights: Pads the shank against your inner leg
Easy to fit to most shanks

p: On a long spar or a day of removals, the shank rubs the inside of your calf with every step. A padded cover softens that contact and cuts down on chafing and bruising, which makes a real difference by the end of the week.
Check that the cover suits your shank shape before ordering. More spur parts are in replacement gaffs and parts.
Fit the cover so it doesn't interfere with the straps, buckles or gaff, and so it can't slide around once the spur is strapped on.
Remove and check under the cover now and then, since it can hide wear or damage on the shank. Inspect spurs before each climb and follow the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133.

faq.q: Will the Weaver shank cover fit non-Weaver spurs?
faq.a: It may fit other shanks of similar shape. Check the fit so it stays put and doesn't block the straps.

faq.q: Does a shank cover replace upper pads?
faq.a: No. It adds padding along the shank. You still need proper upper pads.

name: Buckingham Velcro Lower Straps
title: Buckingham Velcro Lower Climber Straps
meta: Buckingham climber straps with Velcro closure for the lower ankle position. Quick on and off, even tension and a fresh fit for worn climbing spurs.
tagline: Replacement Velcro lower straps for a quick, even fit on your climbing spurs.
summary: Buckingham Velcro lower straps replace the ankle straps on your climbers with hook-and-loop closures. They go on fast, adjust easily and are a good fix when old buckle straps are cracked or stretched.

p: The lower strap holds the stirrup to your boot and keeps the spur from twisting when you step in. A stretched or cracked strap lets the spur roll, which hurts your footing and your confidence. Velcro straps make it easy to get the same snug fit every time.
Check compatibility with your climbers before ordering. More parts are in replacement gaffs and parts.
Keep the hook side clean of sawdust and bark, which reduces grip. Check for fraying, cuts and worn stitching before each climb, and replace straps that show damage.
Follow the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133 for spur use, and always climb on spurs with a lanyard or flipline.

faq.q: Do Velcro straps hold as well as buckles?
faq.a: They hold well when clean and in good condition. Replace them when the hook-and-loop wears or clogs.

faq.q: Will these fit non-Buckingham spurs?
faq.a: Check the strap width and attachment against your climbers before ordering.

name: Notch Gecko Quick-Connect Lower Climber Straps
title: Notch Gecko Quick-Connect Lower Climber Straps
h1: Notch Gecko Quick-Connect Lower Climber Straps
meta: Notch Gecko climber straps with quick-connect fittings for the lower ankle position on Gecko spurs. Fast on and off and a snug fit. Care and fit tips.
tagline: Quick-connect ankle straps for getting in and out of Gecko spurs fast.
summary: These Notch Gecko climber straps fit the lower position on Gecko spurs and use quick-connect fittings so you can get in and out of the spurs fast. They also serve as direct replacements when original straps wear out.
highlights: Fast on and off between climbs

p: On a removal day you may strap in and out of spurs several times. Quick-connect lower straps speed that up while still holding the stirrup tight to your boot so the spur doesn't twist.
These are made for Gecko spurs. Other parts are in replacement gaffs and parts.
Check webbing, stitching and fittings before each climb. Clear grit from the connectors and replace straps that are frayed, cut or slipping.
Follow Notch's instructions and ANSI Z133, and always use a lanyard or flipline while climbing on spurs.

faq.q: Do these fit other brands of spurs?
faq.a: They are designed for Notch Gecko climbers. Check with the maker before fitting to others.

faq.q: Are upper straps included?
faq.a: These are lower straps. Upper straps are sold separately.

name: Weaver Lower Synthetic Climber Straps
title: Weaver Lower Synthetic Climber Straps
meta: Weaver climber straps in synthetic material for the lower ankle position. Hold up to wet and sap, resist stretching and keep your spurs tight to the boot.
tagline: Synthetic ankle straps that shrug off wet and keep spurs tight to your boot.
summary: Weaver lower synthetic climber straps replace worn ankle straps on your spurs with a synthetic material that handles wet conditions and resists stretching better than old leather. A cheap way to make a set of spurs feel solid again.

p: Leather straps stretch when wet, stiffen when they dry and crack over time. Synthetic straps stay closer to their original length, clean up easily and don't need conditioning. That keeps the stirrup locked to your boot.
Check that the width suits your climbers. More parts are in replacement gaffs and parts.
Before each climb, check straps for cuts, fraying and worn holes, and make sure buckles close and hold. Replace straps at the first sign of damage.
Follow the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, and always climb on spurs with a lanyard or flipline.

faq.q: Will these fit non-Weaver spurs?
faq.a: They may fit spurs with a similar stirrup. Check the width and buckle before ordering.

faq.q: Are synthetic straps better than leather?
faq.a: They handle wet better and stretch less, but either works if kept in good condition.

name: Yale Long Shot Throwline
title: Yale Long Shot Throw Line for Setting Climbing Lines
meta: Yale Long Shot throw line is a slick, low-stretch line for setting climbing and rigging lines high in the canopy. Pair with a throw weight and line cube.
tagline: Slick, low-stretch throw line for clean, high shots into the canopy.
summary: Yale Long Shot throw line is a slick, low-stretch line built to run fast off a cube and slide easily over limbs when you set climbing and rigging lines. It is a go-to for climbers who want consistent high shots.
highlights: Slick coating runs fast over limbs
Low stretch for control when isolating unions
Pairs with throw weights and line cubes

p: Your throw line decides how high and how cleanly a shot goes. A slick line pays out without dragging, and slides over bark and through tight crotches when you isolate a union. Long Shot is built for that, and its low stretch gives you better feel when you work the line through the canopy.
Pair it with a throw weight that suits the height and a cube or bag that lets the line run free. More options are in throw line.
Flake the line into the cube carefully after each use so the next shot runs clean. Keep it out of sawdust and dirt, and replace sections that are fuzzed, flattened or cut.

Throw line is not life support. Use it only to install climbing and rigging lines. Clear the drop zone before every throw, stay well away from power lines, and inspect your tie-in point before climbing in line with ANSI Z133.

faq.q: What weight should I use with Yale Long Shot?
faq.a: Most climbers use 10 to 16 oz weights depending on height and conditions. Lighter weights travel farther on a slick line; heavier ones push through dense canopy.

faq.q: Can I climb or rig on throw line?
faq.a: No. Throw line is only for pulling up climbing or rigging lines.

name: Yellow Polyethylene Throwline
title: Yellow Polyethylene Throw Line for Arborists
meta: Yellow polyethylene throw line: a budget-friendly, high-visibility line for setting climbing and rigging lines. Easy to spot, slick and simple to manage.
tagline: High-visibility, budget-friendly throw line for everyday line setting.
summary: This yellow polyethylene throw line is an affordable, high-visibility line for setting climbing and rigging lines. The bright color is easy to track in the canopy and on the ground, and polyethylene is light and slick.
highlights: Easy to spot in leaf litter

p: Not every job needs premium throw line. For crews who lose or cut a lot of line, an affordable polyethylene line in high-visibility yellow does the job, and the color makes it easy to see where the shot landed and to pick it back out of brush.
Pair it with a throw weight and a cube or bag. More options are in throw line.
Polyethylene can be springier than coated premium lines, so flake it carefully into the cube to avoid tangles. Replace sections that are cut, melted from friction or heavily abraded.

Throw line is never life support. Use it only to install climbing and rigging lines, clear the drop zone before throwing, keep away from power lines, and inspect your tie-in point before climbing as required by ANSI Z133.

faq.q: Is polyethylene throw line as good as coated line?
faq.a: It works for most jobs and costs less. Coated lines tend to run slicker and tangle less.

faq.q: Why choose yellow?
faq.a: It is easy to see in the canopy and on the ground, which saves time on each shot.

name: Notch Throw Weight
title: Notch Throw Weight for Setting Climbing Lines
meta: Notch throw weight for setting throw line high in the canopy. Durable shell, bright color and a ring to tie to. Choose the weight that suits your trees.
tagline: A tough, bright throw weight for setting line in big and small trees.
summary: The Notch throw weight is a durable shot-filled bag for launching throw line into the canopy. Its tough shell and bright color stand up to repeat throws and are easy to find in the brush.

p: A good throw weight flies straight, survives hitting branches and the ground, and is easy to find when the shot goes wide. Notch weights have a tough shell and a ring to tie your throw line to, and come in several weights so you can match the bag to the tree.

Throw weights work best with a slick throw line and a cube or bag that lets the line pay out without tangling. Different weights suit different heights and line diameters, so many climbers carry two. See all options in throw weight and line.
Tie the throw line with a secure knot and check the ring and shell for wear before each use. Retire a bag that is split or leaking shot.

Clear the drop zone and call out before every throw. Keep people, vehicles and power lines well clear, and never throw near energized conductors. Once the line is set, pull your climbing line up and inspect the union and the tie-in point before you climb, following ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions.

faq.q: What weight should I choose?
faq.a: Lighter weights go higher on a thin line in open canopy; heavier ones punch through dense branches. Many climbers carry two sizes.

faq.q: How do I attach throw line?
faq.a: Tie it to the ring with a secure knot such as a clove hitch backed up or a bowline.

name: Weaver 12 oz Throw Weight
title: Weaver 12 oz Throw Weight for Arborist Throw Line
meta: Weaver 12 oz throw weight, a mid-weight bag for setting throw line in most trees. Tough vinyl shell, ring for tying in and bright color for easy recovery.
tagline: A mid-weight throw bag that handles most everyday line-setting.
summary: The Weaver 12 oz throw weight is a mid-range bag that suits most trees, heavy enough to carry line through light canopy and light enough to reach good height. It has a ring to tie your throw line to and a bright, durable shell.

p: Twelve ounces is a common all-rounder. It carries enough momentum to pull most throw lines over a high limb and drop back to the ground, without being so heavy that height suffers.

Throw weights work best with a slick throw line and a cube or bag that lets the line pay out without tangling. Different weights suit different heights and line diameters, so many climbers carry two. See all options in throw weight and line.
